_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 5 Mathematics unit lecture film, Real Life. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. REVISED 2026-09-25: the previous version invented all three of its worked examples (213 sh x 4 = 852; 356 / 4 = 89; 65 x 6 = 390) and all three choosing-a-method sums (7+5, 34+58, 236+458), justified by the lesson's own self-check claiming 5Ni.04 and 5Ni.05 against W p85, a workbook page outside this app. Verified: the lesson's own 27 word problems (real-life.html PROBLEMS array) sort into seven tools - extend (8), square (7), factors (4), rule (3), percent (2), pattern (2), round (1) - and NOT ONE is an estimate-and-multiply or estimate-and-divide problem in the sense 5Ni.04/5Ni.05 require (round first, then multiply/divide a number up to 1000 by a 1- or 2-digit number). The lesson's only genuinely 'roundable' numbers either are not multiplications at all (27,849 rounds to 28,000, a plain rounding problem) or exceed the 1000 ceiling (2,024 pencils / 8 crates). Its square/cube/root problems (patio 7x7=49, rug root-144=12, block tower 4 cubed=64, orange crate cube-root-125=5, square garden root-64=8) use small factors (4,5,7,8,12) that make a rounding-based estimate misleading rather than useful - rounding 7 up to 10 to estimate 7x7 gives 100 against an exact 49, more than double, which is not 'close to the estimate' and would have been a false demonstration of the method. So this film drops 5Ni.04 and 5Ni.05 rather than reinvent worked examples for them, and is rebuilt entirely from the lesson's own numbers: the patio, rug, garden and block-tower square/cube problems for 'Choosing a method' and 'A square, the other way round'; the orange crate's own trial-and-improvement (try 4, too few; try 5, exact) for 'Estimating first', since that IS the lesson's own guess-then-check method, unlike a rounding estimate the small factors cannot support; Amina's savings and the pencil-boxes division for the jottings/formal examples; and the block tower read end to end for 'Reading the story'. Every number said here appears in real-life.html's own PROBLEMS array and is solved by the method the lesson itself uses for it.
title: Real Life
subtitle: Grade 5 Mathematics

beats.say: A word problem hides its numbers inside a story. First, you choose a method.

at.hides: hides its numbers inside a story

beats.say: Estimate first, then decide: mentally, with jottings, or a full formal method.
Some calculations are quick enough to do in your head, with no working needed.

at.quick: quick enough to do in your head

beats.say: 7 times 7 is 49 - a patio's tiles, worked out in your head.
Bigger numbers need jottings - quick notes to hold your steps.

at.notes: quick notes to hold your steps

beats.say: Amina saves 250 shillings, then 5 more weeks of 50: 500 shillings.
The hardest calculations need a full formal method, step by step.
2,024 pencils shared into boxes of 8 makes exactly 253 boxes.
Picking the right method is part of solving any problem.
Before the exact answer, make a sensible first guess.
A crate holds 125 oranges, packed as a solid cube.
Try 4 along each edge: 4 times 4 times 4 makes 64.
That is too few - so try one more: 5 along each edge.
5 times 5 times 5 makes exactly 125 oranges, with nothing left over.
A first guess is not the exact answer - just a sensible start.
Then check: does your exact answer match the story?
Estimating first catches a mistake before you finish the sum.

at.catches: catches a mistake before you finish the sum

scenes.heading: A square, the other way round

beats.say: A square rug is made from 144 small tiles.
How many tiles run along one edge? Try 12 tiles.

at.howmany: How many tiles run along one edge

beats.say: 12 times 12 makes 144 - so 12 tiles along each edge.
A square garden covers 64 square metres in total.
8 times 8 makes 64 - so each side is 8 metres.
A square number works both ways: find the whole, or find the side.
Any square number is made by multiplying one whole number by itself.

at.itself: multiplying one whole number by itself

beats.say: A solid cube is built from small blocks, 4 along every edge.
First, find the numbers: 4 blocks, along every edge.
Next, find the real question: how many blocks in the whole cube?

at.wholecube: how many blocks in the whole cube

beats.say: One layer is 4 rows of 4: 4 times 4 makes 16 blocks.
Four layers stacked up: 16 times 4 makes 64 blocks in all.
Multiplying is the right tool once you know the numbers.
Read the story first, then choose the tool that fits it.

at.choosetool: choose the tool that fits it

beats.say: Choose your method: mentally, with jottings, or a full formal method.
Make a sensible first guess, then check your exact answer.
12 times 12 is 144. 4 times 4 times 4 is 64.
Always read the story first, then pick the tool that fits.
The same two moves work on any of the twenty-seven problems.
